Before You Buy a Sub-Sale Home: What to Check

A viewing takes twenty minutes. The consequences last decades. Here is what to look at — and what you cannot see without instruments.

30 May 20266 min readGO XPERT SOLUTION

Unlike a new unit, a sub-sale home comes with no defect liability period. Whatever is wrong on the day you sign becomes yours to fix. That makes the viewing — and what you do before signing — far more consequential.

Go during the day, and go twice if you can

Daylight reveals uneven finishes, damp patches and staining that evening viewings hide. A second visit after heavy rain tells you more than any question you can ask the seller.

What to look at yourself

  • Ceiling corners and junctions — old stains often mean past or current leaks
  • Under sinks and around water heaters — look for corrosion and past drips
  • Wall bases — efflorescence, that white powdery salt, indicates moisture movement
  • Window and door operation — open and close every one
  • Floor level — a marble or a ball will find slopes you cannot see
  • The distribution board — is it labelled, does it look ageing or modified?

Ask about renovations

Ask what was renovated and when. Hacked walls, relocated pipes and added electrical points are where problems concentrate — especially if the work was done without proper method.

A repainted wall is not always cosmetic. Fresh paint on one wall in an otherwise older house is worth asking about.

What you cannot see at a viewing

This is where an inspection earns its cost. Moisture inside walls, failed earthing, hidden leaks, insulation and wiring condition — none of these are visible, and all of them are expensive.

Thermal imaging and moisture meters find them without opening anything. Electrical testing gives you measured values instead of assumptions.

Use the findings before you sign

An inspection report with repair cost estimates changes the conversation with the seller. You are no longer negotiating on impressions — you are discussing specific defects with specific costs attached.

And occasionally the report tells you the most valuable thing of all: that this particular house is not worth the asking price.
